# Reference scaling suites: Pythia and Cerebras-GPT

These are designed scaling suites, not labs with an experiments-vs-final split. They give clean
reference curves on a public dataset (the Pile) against which the lab chapters can be read.
Working notes with sources are in `data/notes/reference.md`.

```{python}
#| echo: false
from src.chapter import *  # noqa
import numpy as np
```

## Cerebras-GPT: a published law and its out-of-sample point

Seven sizes from 111M to 13B, each trained on about 20 tokens per parameter. Cerebras fitted a
loss-versus-compute law on the six smaller models and reports that the 13B landed within 0.5
percent of it. We treat the 13B as the out-of-sample "final run" and draw both Cerebras's own
law (grey, from the paper) and our refit on the same six points.

```{python}
df_c = load.runs("cerebras", "cerebras-gpt")
df_c = df_c[~df_c["run_id"].str.contains("mup")].drop_duplicates("run_id").copy()
df_c.loc[df_c["run_id"] == "cerebras-gpt-13b", "run_type"] = "final"
df_c["is_final"] = df_c["run_type"] == "final"
fit_c = fits.fit_experiments(df_c, irreducible=True)
# Cerebras's own law, paper Sec. 3.1: L(f) = (f / 5.984e22)^(-0.0737) + 0.5066
stated = fits.stated_fit(E=0.5066, A=5.984e22 ** 0.0737, alpha=0.0737)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
plots.scaling_curve(df_c, fit=fit_c, ax=ax, title="Cerebras-GPT: Pile test loss vs training FLOPs", ylabel="Pile test loss (nats/token)")
xs = np.geomspace(df_c["flops"].min(), df_c["flops"].max() * 3, 100)
ax.plot(xs, stated.predict(xs), color=plots.MUTED, lw=2, ls=(0, (1, 2)), label="Cerebras's published law", zorder=1)
ax.legend(loc="upper right"); plt.show()
res_c = fits.final_residuals(df_c, fit_c)
display(Markdown(f"Our refit on 111M to 6.7B: `{fit_c.label()}`. Cerebras's law: `{stated.label()}`."))
display(res_c.round(4))
```

Two things to carry into the lab chapters. First, Cerebras counts training FLOPs about 1.7 times
higher than the 6ND convention, so any cross-suite overlay needs one convention. Second, the
elasticity of loss with respect to compute at the 13B point is small in absolute terms because
the fitted irreducible term is large; the table above gives the number.

## Pythia: sixteen models, one token stream

70M to 12B, standard and deduplicated Pile, the same 300B tokens in the same order, 154
checkpoints per model. EleutherAI published no numerical loss values, but the W&B project is
public, and the Pile validation loss at the final step of each model's training run is now in
`runs.csv` for 13 of the 16 models (`data/losses/eleutherai/`; the run-to-model mapping is by
matching layer count, width, batch size and data path in the run configs, since the repository's
own mapping is "rough and partial", and no finished deduplicated run matching 1B, 6.9B or 12B was
found). The compute axis is 6ND (total parameters, including untied embeddings).

```{python}
df_p = load.runs("eleutherai", "pythia")
dl = df_p.drop_duplicates("run_id").dropna(subset=["loss", "flops"]).copy()
dl["dedup"] = dl["run_id"].str.contains("deduped")
fit_p = fits.fit_experiments(dl[~dl["dedup"]], irreducible=True)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
for dd, name, c in [(False, "Pile", plots.PROJECT_SLOTS[0]), (True, "Pile deduplicated", plots.PROJECT_SLOTS[1])]:
    s = dl[dl["dedup"] == dd].sort_values("flops")
    ax.plot(s["flops"], s["loss"], color=c, lw=2, marker="o", markersize=7, markeredgecolor=plots.SURFACE, markeredgewidth=1.5, label=name)
if fit_p is not None:
    xs = np.geomspace(dl["flops"].min(), dl["flops"].max(), 100)
    ax.plot(xs, fit_p.predict(xs), color=plots.MUTED, lw=2, ls=(0, (1, 2)), label="fit on the standard-Pile models", zorder=1)
ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_xlabel("Training compute (FLOPs, 6ND)"); ax.set_ylabel("Pile validation loss (nats/token)")
ax.set_title("Pythia: final Pile validation loss vs compute"); ax.legend(loc="upper right"); plt.show()
if fit_p is not None:
    display(Markdown(f"Fit on the standard-Pile models: `{fit_p.label()}`. The deduplicated models sit above the "
                     "standard ones on this axis because their validation set is the deduplicated Pile, a harder target; "
                     "the two series are not one curve."))
```

The benchmark view below uses the released zero-shot evaluation files.

```{python}
bench = "lambada_openai_acc_0shot" if (df_p["benchmark_name"] == "lambada_openai_acc_0shot").any() else df_p["benchmark_name"].dropna().iloc[0]
dp = df_p[df_p["benchmark_name"] == bench].copy()
dp["dedup"] = dp["run_id"].str.contains("deduped")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
for dd, name, c in [(False, "Pile", plots.PROJECT_SLOTS[0]), (True, "Pile deduplicated", plots.PROJECT_SLOTS[1])]:
    s = dp[dp["dedup"] == dd].sort_values("flops")
    ax.plot(s["flops"], s["benchmark_value"], color=c, lw=2, marker="o", markersize=7, markeredgecolor=plots.SURFACE, markeredgewidth=1.5, label=name)
ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_xlabel("Training compute (FLOPs, 6ND)"); ax.set_ylabel(bench.replace("_", " "))
ax.set_title("Pythia: zero-shot accuracy vs compute, two data variants"); ax.legend(loc="lower right"); plt.show()
```

```{python}
gh = df_p.drop_duplicates("run_id")["gpu_hours"].sum()
display(Markdown(f"Reported A100-hours for the sixteen released models: **{gh:,.0f}**. The paper's total including the "
                 "discarded first version of the suite is 544,280, so about three quarters of the suite's compute went into "
                 "the released models. That discarded suite is a rare published example of experiment compute that would "
                 "otherwise be invisible."))
```

## Both suites on one compute axis

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
plots.overlay_projects({"Cerebras-GPT (reported FLOPs, Pile test)": df_c, "Pythia (6ND FLOPs, Pile validation)": dl[~dl["dedup"]]},
                       {"Cerebras-GPT (reported FLOPs, Pile test)": fit_c, "Pythia (6ND FLOPs, Pile validation)": fit_p}, ax=ax,
                       title="Reference suites: Pile loss vs compute")
plt.show()
```

The two suites are close but not on one curve: Cerebras reports Pile *test* loss and counts FLOPs
about 1.7x above 6ND; Pythia's number is the trainer's Pile *validation* loss at the last step,
on 6ND compute. Both use the GPT-NeoX tokenizer, so the nats-per-token scale is shared.
